summary.value: The paper solves Nash equilibrium in two-player zero-sum extensive-form games by adding additional regularization. By switching the reference strategy periodically, the algorithm converges to the NE of the original game rather than the regularized game. The paper proves convergence theoretically and empirically evaluates its performance.

strengths.value:
- The presentation is clear and easy to follow
- The paper includes deep learning experiments and achieves better performance compared to the baselines

weaknesses.value:
My major concern is that the comparison with previous work is not enough. The most relevant paper I can think of, [1], is not included in this paper.

[1] added additional regularization and changed the reference strategy periodically. Moreover, [1] had theoretical guarantees on convergence.

[1] Abe, Kenshi, et al. "Adaptively perturbed mirror descent for learning in games." arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.16610 (2023).

questions.value: See weaknesses. May the authors explain the main contribution of this paper compared to [1]? I would be happy to re-evaluate the paper if the authors could clarify this.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission2942 by Reviewer CmAX

comment.value:
Thank you for pointing out our oversight regarding [1]. At the time of writing, we were not aware of this work. As it turns out, their method is theoretically equivalent to ours (they use a different mirror descent update but obtain the same update direction). We will reposition our paper accordingly and include a more thorough comparison with prior work (including [1], DeepNash, etc.). Our work can be viewed as extending [1] to the MARL setting, and we believe our contribution remains meaningful by demonstrating that NashPG is an effective MARL algorithm that is both efficient and simple to implement. Although [1] may supersede our theoretical contribution, we hope our empirical findings provide useful value to the community.

[1] Abe, Kenshi, et al. "Adaptively perturbed mirror descent for learning in games." arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.16610 (2023).

replying_to: Replying to Nash Policy Gradient: A Policy Gradient Method with Iteratively Refined Regularization for Finding Nash Equilibria
display_title: Official Review of Submission2942 by Reviewer yAWv

summary.value: This paper introduces Nash Policy Gradient (NashPG), a novel algorithm for finding Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games. The authors fix regularization at a large value for stability and achieve convergence through iterative refinement of a reference policy. Theoretically, the authors showed that NashPG demonstrates monotonic improvement and convergence to the Nash equilibrium. Experiments on benchmark and imperfect-information games show that NashPG not only exhibit faster convergence, but also achieves lower exploitability and higher Elo ratings than population-based and CFR-inspired baselines.

strengths.value:
The idea of iterative refinement under fixed regularization strength was not previously explored in MARL. The analytical results seem rigorous and intuitive to the reviewer.
The empirical evaluation of NashPG is not limited to toy examples to validate the theoretical result. The authors also included more complicated games with imperfect information to demonstrate the performance and effectiveness of NashPG compared to baseline methods.
The paper is well written with clear motivations, and the theoretical and experimental results are also presented in a concise and readable manner.

weaknesses.value:
Although the authors did provide a theoretical analysis, no convergence guarantees in finite time were provided; instead, there were only a few lemmas. This significantly hurt the theoretical contribution of this work, especially since existing policy gradient algorithms such as [1] have been shown to guarantee convergence to NE in finite time. The author also did not cite this paper and a few other closely related works.
[1] Zhang, Kaiqing, et al. "Model-based multi-agent RL in zero-sum Markov games with near-optimal sample complexity." Journal of Machine Learning Research 24.175 (2023): 1-53.

The authors should include synthetic examples in order to show convergence properties. Current experiments are very different from the algorithms in the previous sections. At the very least, the authors should have had experiments demonstrating the monotonic descent properties of NashPG in practice.

questions.value:
- How about multi-agent RL beyond two-player zero-sum?
- How does this compare or relate to the anchor changing algorithm [2] in single-agent RL?
Zhou, Ruida, et al. "Anchor-changing regularized natural policy gradient for multi-objective reinforcement learning." Advances in neural information processing systems 35 (2022): 13584-13596.
- In the experiments, what does the step number represent? Since the proposed NashPG is a dual-loop method, whereas some other baseline methods are single-loop. Does step number represent T or KT? It could be an unfair advantage for the other algorithms. A better approach is to compare the number of gradient calculations across different algorithms.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission2942 by Reviewer yAWv

comment.value:
Thank you for your kind words regarding the presentation, analysis, and experimental depth of our work. We invested significant effort to ensure the paper is accessible and to include non-trivial environments in the experiments.

**Regarding the novelty of iterative refinement:**
To be fair, DeepNash [1] employs a similar iterative-regularization idea and updates via NeuRD, which can also be viewed as a MARL algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, they are the first to use this idea in MARL.

Our experiments focus on the practical version of our algorithm, NashPG, and its effectiveness in large and complex domains. While toy examples illustrating convergence would be valuable, we believe our theoretical proof provides adequate justification. As highlighted by reviewer CmAX, [2] presents an algorithm equivalent to our theoretical method and additionally provides finite-time guarantees, which supersede our theoretical contribution.

**On multi-agent settings beyond two-player zero-sum:**
Evaluating multi-agent general-sum MARL is even more challenging. In this work, we restrict our focus to two-player zero-sum games.

On the relation to anchor-changing algorithms [3]:
We are not very familiar with this line of work, though it appears to share a similar idea of modifying regularization. Our analysis focuses mainly on comparing to MARL algorithms.

**On the definition of “step”:**
A “step” represents one parameter update. We ensure that all methods use the same number of parameter updates and the same number of environment interactions. (PSRO uses slightly more environment steps due to computing the meta-game matrix, but this difference is minor.)

[1] Julien Perolat, et al. Mastering the game of Stratego with model-free multiagent reinforcement learning. Science, 2022.
[2] Abe, Kenshi, et al. "Adaptively perturbed mirror descent for learning in games." arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.16610 (2023).
[3] Zhou, Ruida, et al. "Anchor-changing regularized natural policy gradient for multi-objective reinforcement learning." NeurIPS 2022.

replying_to: Replying to Nash Policy Gradient: A Policy Gradient Method with Iteratively Refined Regularization for Finding Nash Equilibria
display_title: Official Review of Submission2942 by Reviewer EUnL

summary.value: This paper examines regularization-based equilibrium finding in two-player zero-sum games. The paper proves that iteratively replacing the reference policy in Magnetic Mirror Descent (MMD) with the fixed-point policy of the last learning round guarantees monotonic improvement and last-iterate convergence towards Nash equilibrium (NE). Based on this finding, the paper proposes a reinforcement learning algorithm called Nash Policy Gradient (NashPG) that iteratively reduces the exploitability of the learned policy for practically solving large-scale games. Experiments in benchmark or real-world games demonstrate the superiority of NashPG over MMD and average-iterate-based algorithms like Neural Fictitious Self-Play (NFSP) and Policy-Space Response Oracles (PSRO).

strengths.value:
1. This paper is well-written and easy to follow. The background of solving regularized variational inequalities is well-introduced.

2. The theoretical results of iterative improvement are clearly demonstrated without assuming interior or unique NE.

3. The construction of NashPG is elegant, making the algorithm generally applicable under different single-agent RL algorithms.

4. Extensive experiments convince me that NashPG is efficient. The choices of performance measure are also reasonably explained.

weaknesses.value:
1. The idea of iteratively replacing the reference policy is not that novel in view of the existing literature [1,2,3,4] in the field of equilibrium finding.

2. More recent RL algorithms for solving imperfect-information games (like NeuRD [5]) could also be considered as comparative methods.

[1] Julien Perolat, et al. From Poincare recurrence to convergence in imperfect information games: Finding equilibrium via regularization. ICML, 2021.

[2] Kenshi Abe, et al. Mutation-driven follow the regularized leader for last-iterate convergence in zero-sum games. UAI, 2022.

[3] Kenshi Abe, et al. Adaptively perturbed mirror descent for learning in games. ICML, 2024.

[4] Runyu Lu, et al. Divergence-regularized discounted aggregation: Equilibrium finding in multiplayer partially observable stochastic games. ICLR, 2025.

[5] Julien Perolat, et al. Mastering the game of Stratego with model-free multiagent reinforcement learning. Science, 2022.

questions.value:
1. Could you compare the theoretical results with references [1,2,3,4] to further explain what leads to the advantage of your theory?

2. Could you also compare NashPG with NeuRD [5] or explain the reason why you prefer not to compare it in the experiment?

comment.value:
Thank you for your positive feedback regarding the clarity of our paper. We aimed to ensure it is accessible to a broad set of readers. We also appreciate your acknowledgment of our experimental setup, as choosing appropriate metrics and environments is nontrivial due to the lack of standard benchmarks in MARL. We hope our work contributes to making the field more unified.

We acknowledge that iterative refinement of regularization exists in prior work. We will expand the introduction and related-work sections to properly discuss these methods and include a comparison table as suggested by reviewer ztpz. As reviewer CmAX noted, our theoretical algorithm is equivalent to [1], which also provides a finite-time bound and therefore supersedes our theoretical contribution. We will reposition our work as an extension of [1] to the MARL setting.

**Regarding comparison with NeuRD [5]:**
We agree that NeuRD is a relevant baseline. However, we believe comparing to DeepNash (R-NaD) would be even more suitable, since it uses a similar idea of iterative refinement with NeuRD updates. We attempted to include this comparison, but the implementation difficulty was substantial. We will add an explicit remark about this and list it as future work.

[1] Abe, Kenshi, et al. "Adaptively perturbed mirror descent for learning in games." arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.16610 (2023).

replying_to: Replying to Nash Policy Gradient: A Policy Gradient Method with Iteratively Refined Regularization for Finding Nash Equilibria
display_title: Official Review of Submission2942 by Reviewer ztpz

summary.value: Regularized Nash equilibriums are easier to compute compared their non-regularized counterpart but are exploitable in the original game. There exists a body of works that try to shrink this gap. Commonly, this is done via temperature decay. Unfortunately, lower temperatures are often unstable and converge slowly. R-NaD and FoReL proposed to iteratively regularize to the previous Nash equilibrium in an iterative process. This work proposes a policy space version of the same result.

strengths.value: On the more material side of things, the paper is well written, the accompanying Jax codebase is also easy to read. The paper proposes a natural way of updating the magnet of MMD which has been used successfully in R-NaD.

weaknesses.value:
The theoretical results are not exciting. They are equivalent to the theorems of R-NaD (FoReL) but for mirror decent instead of follow the regularized leader (FTRL).

The experiments are questionable. For starters, the choice of using a linear policy is questionable. This is particularly concerning as the results do not match, for instance those of Rudolph et al 2025 (cited @965).  Calculating exploitability with neural networks has been shown to be extremely unreliable but the authors do not measure it for the 4 games @ 413 even thought exploitability calculation is readily available. Plotting standard deviation with 4 samples is somewhat questionable. Negative exploitability is a clear indicator of  bug or learning issues. In the worst case it should be zero by initializing the best response policies with the best policy available. The use of ELO for hold'em is questionable as the average win points is the quantity of interest. Similarly, given that imperfect information games are cyclic in nature, the use of ELO is also questionable. In all cases EVs should have been reported instead. Furthermore, for hold'em, a comparison with slumbot is necessary to gauge the strength of the policy. The "real games" are not necessary real games, for liars dice, the 6th dice is missing and the observations are not open spiel compatible.

questions.value:
I think the paper would strongly benefit from having a table of sort describing the different contribution of this work vs mmd vs R-NaD (deep Nash, FoReL, etc).

Why are the MMD experiment ran with PPO? Is it unreasonable to do vanilla policy gradient directly? This is the first MMD implementation I've seen that uses PPO.

The claim @206 that the need to decrease learning rate must decrease with temperature is problematic is not evaluated. As the temperature decreases the movement of the regularized Nash also decreases (at least empirically) as it moves on a finite curve from the objective with alpha_0 regularization to the maximum entropy objective with no entropy. Are there any evidence that these vanishing step sizes are problematic?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission2942 by Reviewer ztpz

comment.value:
Thank you for your positive comments on the clarity of our writing and codebase. We put considerable effort into making both accessible.

We understand the comment that our theoretical results are essentially equivalent to those of R-NaD (FoReL), but formulated under mirror descent instead of FTRL. However, we would like to emphasize that NashPG and R-NaD, despite sharing the iterative-regularization idea, are distinct algorithms that lead to quite different implementations. We believe extending the idea via mirror descent to produce a much simpler policy-gradient-based update is a useful theoretical contribution. That said, as reviewer CmAX noted, our theoretical algorithm (the “MMD-based Iterative M Method”) is very similar to APMD [1], which we were not aware of during writing. Their algorithm uses a different mirror-descent update but ultimately yields the same descent direction, and they additionally provide a finite-time bound, superseding our theoretical contribution.

**Regarding the experiments:**
To clarify: Table 3 summarizes our model architectures. “Linear” refers to a dense matrix feature extractor; all models still use nonlinearities (ReLU). We intentionally design metrics that generalize to large games. While computing exact exploitability is tractable in simple games, it is intractable in most realistic domains. Therefore, we approximate exploitability via single-agent RL training. To our knowledge, this is the best practical approach in two-player zero-sum games. Negative exploitability can arise when the initial random policy fails to win a single game or when trained with insufficient steps. Since all models receive equal training budgets for their opponents, we believe this comparison remains fair.

Regarding the use of Elo: We are aware of cyclicity issues in imperfect-information games. However, most prior works rely on head-to-head evaluations, which suffer from the same limitations. Elo provides a more aggregated and stable version of this evaluation. Expected value (EV) metrics also depend on the specific population used, making them imperfect as well and only clearly meaningful in Poker-style games.

**On suggested additions:**
We agree that a comparison table summarizing the differences between our method, MMD, and R-NaD (DeepNash, FoReL, etc.) would be valuable and will include one.

**On MMD with PPO:**
It is perfectly reasonable to use vanilla policy gradient; however, the original MMD paper used PPO in the RL setting, and we observed PPO to generally perform better empirically. This motivated our choice.

**On the claim about decreasing learning rates with temperature:**
We conducted a small-scale MMD experiment (@1046) showing that vanishing step sizes lead to poor performance. Typically, decaying step sizes yield slow learning, so we believe this supports our argument.

[1] Abe, Kenshi, et al. "Adaptively perturbed mirror descent for learning in games." arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.16610 (2023).

display_title: Meta Review of Submission2942 by Area Chair nFvi

summary.value:
The paper propose NashPG to finds Nash Equilibria in zero-sum (Markov) games through large regularization but with periodically updated reference policy. The algorithm is proven to have monotonic improvement and last-iterate convergence.     

The novelty has been a common concerns of all reviewers, and the authors also admit that they omitted some prior work whose theoretical framework can supersede the one in this paper.  The experiment part is also not entirely convincing, e.g., negative exploitability and that the applicability of ELO in the considered games.  Overall, the work needs to reposition their work, clarify their contribution, and strengthen their experimental evaluation.

reviewer_concerns.value:
- Novelty (all reviewers) — partially addressed: The iterative regularization algorithmic idea has overlap with  APMD (Abe et al.) and R-NaD, etc.  The theoretical analysis can be superseded by those of in prior work. The author would like to reposition their work as their extension to the MARL setting, and emphasize that their algorithm is mirror descent, which is different from FTRL of R-NaD.  

- Metric validity regarding exploitability and ELO (reviewer ztpz) — partially addressed:  there is negative exploitability value in the experiment, which is not reasonable. Also, ELO is questionable in cyclic games. The author explains that exact exploitability is hard to measure, and that other measures than ELO also suffer similar issue.
